"Easy on Me" has been included in rankings of Adele's discography. *Rolling Stone* named it her 10th-best song in 2021.[[57]](#cite_note-60) *Far Out*'s Tyler Golsen and Jamie Kahn included it at number 17 in 2022.[[58]](#cite_note-61) That same year, *[American Songwriter](/wiki/American_Songwriter "American Songwriter")*'s Tina Benitez-Eves declared "Easy on Me" Adele's best song.[[59]](#cite_note-62) It was included on critical lists of the best songs of 2021, by *Billboard* at number 14,[[60]](#cite_note-63) *The Forty-Five* and *NME* at number 26,[[61]](#cite_note-64)[[62]](#cite_note-65) and *[Consequence](/wiki/Consequence_(publication) "Consequence (publication)")* at number 27.[[63]](#cite_note-66) The song also appeared in an unranked list by *[Vogue](/wiki/Vogue_(magazine) "Vogue (magazine)")*.[[64]](#cite_note-67)

"Easy on Me" received several awards and nominations. It won the [Brit Award for Song of the Year](/wiki/Brit_Award_for_Song_of_the_Year "Brit Award for Song of the Year") at the [2022 ceremony](/wiki/Brit_Awards_2022 "Brit Awards 2022").[[65]](#cite_note-68) That year, "Easy on Me" also received the [*Gaffa* Award](/wiki/Gaffa_(magazine)#GAFFA_Awards "Gaffa (magazine)") for Foreign Song of the Year,[[66]](#cite_note-69) the [Juno Award for Video of the Year](/wiki/Juno_Award_for_Video_of_the_Year "Juno Award for Video of the Year"),[[67]](#cite_note-70) and the [New Music Award](/wiki/New_Music_Award "New Music Award") for Top 40/CHR Song of the Year.[[68]](#cite_note-71) At the [65th Annual Grammy Awards](/wiki/65th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "65th Annual Grammy Awards") in 2023, the song won [Best Pop Solo Performance](/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Pop_Solo_Performance "Grammy Award for Best Pop Solo Performance") and was nominated for [Record of the Year](/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Record_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Record of the Year"), [Song of the Year](/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Song_of_the_Year "Grammy Award for Song of the Year"), and [Best Music Video](/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Music_Video "Grammy Award for Best Music Video").[[69]](#cite_note-72) Other nominations include The Song

Main article: [Regular octahedron](/wiki/Regular_octahedron "Regular octahedron")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Octahedron.jpg/250px-Octahedron.jpg)](/wiki/File:Octahedron.jpg)

A [regular octahedron](/wiki/Regular_octahedron "Regular octahedron")

The [regular octahedron](/wiki/Regular_octahedron "Regular octahedron") has eight [equilateral triangle](/wiki/Equilateral_triangle "Equilateral triangle") sides, six [vertices](/wiki/Vertex_(geometry) "Vertex (geometry)") at which four sides meet, and twelve edges. Its [dual polyhedron](/wiki/Dual_polyhedron "Dual polyhedron") is a [cube](/wiki/Cube "Cube").[[1]](#cite_note-1) It can be formed as the [convex hull](/wiki/Convex_hull "Convex hull") of the six axis-parallel [unit vectors](/wiki/Unit_vector "Unit vector") in three-dimensional [Euclidean space](/wiki/Euclidean_space "Euclidean space"). It is one of the five [Platonic solids](/wiki/Platonic_solid "Platonic solid"),[[2]](#cite_note-2) and the three-dimensional case of an infinite family of [regular polytopes](/wiki/Regular_polytope "Regular polytope"), the [cross polytopes](/wiki/Cross_polytope "Cross polytope").[[3]](#cite_note-3) Although it does not tile space by itself, it can tile space together with the [regular tetrahedron](/wiki/Regular_tetrahedron "Regular tetrahedron") to form the [tetrahedral-octahedral honeycomb](/wiki/Tetrahedral-octahedral_honeycomb "Tetrahedral-octahedral honeycomb").[[4]](#cite_note-4)

fanoutqa_007398.t: Thomas Jefferson :: Interests and activities :: Inventions :: chunk_0053
fanoutqa_007398.x:
Thomas Jefferson :: Interests and activities :: Inventions :: chunk_0053
Jefferson invented many small practical devices and improved contemporary inventions, including a revolving book-stand and a "Great Clock" powered by the gravitational pull on cannonballs. He improved the [pedometer](/wiki/Pedometer "Pedometer"), the [polygraph](/wiki/Polygraph_(duplicating_device) "Polygraph (duplicating device)") (a device for duplicating writing),[[445]](#cite_note-467) and the [moldboard plow](/wiki/Moldboard_plow "Moldboard plow"), an idea he never patented and gave to posterity.[[446]](#cite_note-468) Jefferson can also be credited as the creator of the [swivel chair](/wiki/Swivel_chair#Origin "Swivel chair"), the first of which he created and used to write much of the Declaration of Independence.[[447]](#cite_note-469) He first opposed patents but later supported them. From 1790 to 1793, as Secretary of State, he was the *ex officio* head of the three-person patent review board. He drafted reforms of US patent law which led to him being relieved of this duty in 1793, and also drastically changed the patent system.[[448]](#cite_note-470)

As Minister to France, Jefferson was impressed by the military standardization program known as the *[Système Gribeauval](/wiki/Gribeauval_system "Gribeauval system")*, and initiated a program as president to develop [interchangeable parts](/wiki/Interchangeable_parts "Interchangeable parts") for firearms. For his inventiveness and ingenuity, Jefferson was awarded an honorary Doctor of Law degree from [Harvard University](/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") in 1787.[[449]](#cite_note-471)

The **Empire State Building** is a 102-story,[[c]](#cite_note-Floor_count-10) [supertall](/wiki/Supertall "Supertall") skyscraper in the [Midtown South](/wiki/Midtown_South "Midtown South") neighborhood of [Manhattan](/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"), New York City, United States. The building was designed in the [Art Deco](/wiki/Art_Deco "Art Deco") style by [Shreve, Lamb & Harmon](/wiki/Shreve,_Lamb_%26_Harmon "Shreve, Lamb & Harmon") and constructed between 1930 and 1931. Its name is derived from "[Empire State](/wiki/Empire_State "Empire State")", the [nickname](/wiki/List_of_U.S._state_nicknames "List of U.S. state nicknames") of New York state. The building has a roof height of 1,250 feet (380 m) and stands a total of 1,454 feet (443.2 m) tall including its [antenna](/wiki/Antenna_(radio) "Antenna (radio)"). The Empire State Building was the world's tallest building until the [North Tower](/wiki/1_World_Trade_Center_(1970%E2%80%932001) "1 World Trade Center (1970–2001)") of the [World Trade Center](/wiki/World_Trade_Center_(1973%E2%80%932001) "World Trade Center (1973–2001)") was [topped out in 1970](/wiki/Construction_of_the_World_Trade_Center "Construction of the World Trade Center"); following the [September 11 attacks](/wiki/Collapse_of_the_World_Trade_Center "Collapse of the World Trade Center") in 2001, the Empire State Building was once more New York City's tallest building until it was surpassed in 2012 by [One World Trade Center](/wiki/One_World_Trade_Center "One World Trade Center"). As of 2025, the building is the [eighth-tallest building in New York City](/wiki/List_of_tallest_buildings_in_New_York_City "List of tallest buildings in New York City"), the [tenth-tallest completed skyscraper in the United States](/wiki/List_of_tallest_buildings_in_the_United_States "List of tallest buildings in the United States"), and the [59th-tallest completed skyscraper in the world](/wiki/List_of_tallest_buildings "List of tallest buildings").

Up to and including the [64th Grammy Awards](/wiki/64th_Annual_Grammy_Awards "64th Annual Grammy Awards"), all spoken word recordings fell under one category, the [Best Spoken Word Album](/wiki/Best_Spoken_Word_Album "Best Spoken Word Album"). As of 2023, the Spoken Word category has been renamed **Best Audio Book, Narration & Storytelling Recording**. This category recognizes excellence in spoken word albums, but no longer includes spoken word poetry. The category was authored by and created due to six years of advocacy within the Recording Academy by poet J. Ivy, who then went on to win the first two year's of the category's existence.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

Breast cancer screening can be instrumental, given that the size of a breast cancer and its spread are among the most critical factors in predicting the prognosis of the disease. Breast cancers found during screening are typically smaller and less likely to have spread outside the breast.[[10]](#cite_note-10) Training health workers to do clinical breast examination may have potential to detect breast cancer at an early stage.[[11]](#cite_note-11) A 2013 [Cochrane review](/wiki/Cochrane_review "Cochrane review") found that it was unclear whether [mammographic](/wiki/Mammograph "Mammograph") screening does more harm than good, in that a large proportion of women who test positive turn out not to have the disease.[[12]](#cite_note-Got2013-12) A 2009 review for the [US Preventive Services Task Force](/wiki/US_Preventive_Services_Task_Force "US Preventive Services Task Force") found evidence of benefit in those 40 to 70 years of age,[[13]](#cite_note-13) and the organization recommends screening every two years in women ages 50 to 74.[[14]](#cite_note-USPSTFScreen2016-14)

The medications [tamoxifen](/wiki/Tamoxifen "Tamoxifen") or [raloxifene](/wiki/Raloxifene "Raloxifene") may be used in an effort to prevent breast cancer in those who are at high risk of developing it.[[2]](#cite_note-WCR2014-2) [Surgical removal of both breasts](/wiki/Preventive_mastectomy "Preventive mastectomy") is another preventive measure in some high risk women.[[2]](#cite_note-WCR2014-2) In those who have been diagnosed with cancer, several treatments may be used, including surgery, [radiation therapy](/wiki/Radiation_therapy "Radiation therapy"), [chemotherapy](/wiki/Chemotherapy "Chemotherapy"), [hormonal therapy](/wiki/Hormonal_therapy_(oncology) "Hormonal therapy (oncology)"), and [targeted therapy](/wiki/Targeted_therapy "Targeted therapy").[[1]](#cite_note-NCI2014Pt-1) Types of surgery vary from [breast-conserving surgery](/wiki/Breast-conserving_surgery "Breast-conserving surgery") to [mastectomy](/wiki/Mastectomy "Mastectomy").[[15]](#cite_note-NCI2014TxProf-15) [Breast reconstruction](/wiki/Breast_reconstruction "Breast reconstruction") may t

fanoutqa_037606.x:
Santa Ono :: Early life and education :: chunk_0001
Born in 1962, Santa Ono is the son of Japanese mathematician [Takashi Ono](/wiki/Takashi_Ono_(mathematician) "Takashi Ono (mathematician)"), who immigrated to the United States from Japan in the late 1950s. Ono was born in [Vancouver](/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver"), [British Columbia](/wiki/British_Columbia "British Columbia"), Canada, where his father worked as an assistant professor of mathematics at the University of British Columbia from 1961 to 1964. Ono has United States citizenship and Canadian citizenship.[[1]](#cite_note-bcb-1)

Ono was raised in [Philadelphia, Pennsylvania](/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), and [Towson, Maryland](/wiki/Towson,_Maryland "Towson, Maryland"), where his father worked as a faculty member at the [University of Pennsylvania](/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania") from 1964 to 1969 and at [Johns Hopkins University](/wiki/Johns_Hopkins_University "Johns Hopkins University") from 1969 to 2011, respectively.[[1]](#cite_note-bcb-1)[[6]](#cite_note-6) His older brother is Momoro Ono and his younger brother is [Ken Ono](/wiki/Ken_Ono "Ken Ono").[[7]](#cite_note-7)

Ono received a [Bachelor of Arts](/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") degree with a major in [biological sciences](/wiki/Biological_sciences "Biological sciences") from the [University of Chicago](/wiki/University_of_Chicago "University of Chicago") in 1984 and a [Doctor of Philosophy](/wiki/Doctor_of_Philosophy "Doctor of Philosophy") degree in [experimental medicine](/wiki/Experimental_medicine "Experimental medicine") from [McGill University](/wiki/McGill_University "McGill University") in Canada in 1991.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

At University College London, Ono served as associate dean of students and as a member of the University College London Council.[[9]](#cite_note-Hand-9) From 2006 to 2010, Ono served as senior vice provost for undergraduate education and academic affairs at [Emory University](/wiki/Emory_University "Emory University") in [Atlanta, Georgia](/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta").[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11)

When measured from its traditional source at [Lake Itasca](/wiki/Lake_Itasca "Lake Itasca"), the Mississippi has a length of 2,340 miles (3,766 km). When measured from its longest stream source (most distant source from the sea), [Brower's Spring](/wiki/Brower%27s_Spring "Brower's Spring") in [Montana](/wiki/Montana "Montana"), the source of the [Missouri River](/wiki/Missouri_River "Missouri River"), it has a length of 3,710 miles (5,971 km), making it the fourth longest river in the world after the [Nile](/wiki/Nile "Nile"), [Amazon](/wiki/Amazon_River "Amazon River"), and [Yangtze](/wiki/Yangtze "Yangtze").[[65]](#cite_note-68) When measured by the largest stream source (by water volume), the [Ohio River](/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River"), by extension the [Allegheny River](/wiki/Allegheny_River "Allegheny River"), would be the source, and the Mississippi would begin in [Pennsylvania](/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania").[[66]](#cite_note-69)

Just before a [North London derby](/wiki/North_London_derby "North London derby") between Spurs and Arsenal in 2007.

Initially, football in London was dominated by amateur teams, drawing their membership from former [public schoolboys](/wiki/Public_school_(UK) "Public school (UK)") but gradually working-class sides came to the forefront. Royal Arsenal was London's first professional team, becoming so in 1891,[[9]](#cite_note-10) a move which saw them boycotted by the amateur London Football Association. Other London clubs soon followed Arsenal's footsteps in turning professional, including [Millwall](/wiki/Millwall_F.C. "Millwall F.C.") (1893), [Tottenham Hotspur](/wiki/Tottenham_Hotspur "Tottenham Hotspur") (1895), Fulham (1898) and [West Ham](/wiki/West_Ham_United "West Ham United") (1898).

In the meantime, Woolwich Arsenal (formerly Royal Arsenal) went on to be the first London club to join the Football League, in 1893. The following year, the [Southern League](/wiki/Southern_Football_League "Southern Football League") was founded and many of its members would go on to join the Football League. In 1901 Tottenham Hotspur became the first club from London to win the FA Cup in the professional era, although it would not be until 1931 that a London side would win the Football League, the team in question being Arsenal (having moved to [Highbury](/wiki/Arsenal_Stadium "Arsenal Stadium") in 1913 and dropping the "Woolwich" from their name).

In the [1989–90 season](/wiki/1989%E2%80%9390_Football_League_First_Division#First_Division_maps "1989–90 Football League First Division"), eight of London's professional clubs were in the top tier of English Football at the same time, forming 40% of the [First Division](/wiki/Football_League_First_Division "Football League First Division") that season.

Princeton explicitly prohibited the admission of women from its founding in 1746 until 1969. Since it lacked an affiliated women's college, it was often referred to as a "monastery", both lovingly and derisively, by members of the Princeton community.[[150]](#cite_note-Markham-1962-152)[[151]](#cite_note-153)
For about a decade, from 1887 to 1897, nearby [Evelyn College for Women](/wiki/Evelyn_College_for_Women "Evelyn College for Women") was largely composed of daughters of professors and sisters of Princeton undergraduates. While no legal connection existed, many Princeton professors taught there and several Princeton administrators, such as Francis Patton, were on its board of trustees. It closed in 1897 following the death of its founder, [Joshua McIlvaine](/wiki/Joshua_Hall_McIlvaine "Joshua Hall McIlvaine").[[152]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeitch1978170–171-154)

In 1947, three female members of the library staff enrolled in beginning Russian courses to deal with an increase in Russian literature in the library.[[113]](#cite_note-Princeton-Library-114) In 1961, Princeton admitted its first female graduate student, Sabra Follett Meservey,[[150]](#cite_note-Markham-1962-152) who would go on to be the first woman to earn a master's degree at Princeton.[[113]](#cite_note-Princeton-Library-114) Meservey was, at the time of her admission, already a member of the faculty at Douglass College within Princeton.
